newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles divided over calls to restore death penalty.
newsitem.headline: Poles divided over calls to restore death penalty.

text.p: Poland's interior minister and other key figures in the ruling ex-communist party are backing calls to restore the death penalty after a series of horrific murders, but the prime minister on Tuesday opposed the idea.
"I am convinced the death penalty does not solve problems," Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told public radio when asked to comment on an upsurge of opinion for reviving it.

On Monday thousands of citizens marched through Warsaw in a protest against criminal violence, prompted by the torture and killing this month of a 19-year-old student by a gang angry that he had attended a picnic in woodlands they viewed as their turf.

Interior Minister Leszek Miller urged revival of the death penalty, which had been effectively suspended since just before the 1989 fall of communism and was scrapped in a new criminal code approved by parliament this month.
"I want all these beasts in human skin who kill peaceful people to understand that they could also lose their lives," Miller said in comments quoted by Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

Several of Miller's fellow ex-communist deputies, mindful of voters' opinion before September 21 general elections, backed his call and his Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party said it would leave the decision to members' consciences.
But Cimoszewicz, who heads the party's election campaign said there was no proof the death penalty was a deterrent and argued for society to address the wider origins of violent crime.
He also rejected arguments that it was expensive to keep killers in prison for long sentences, saying: "I think this a dramatic trivialisation of the issue."
The spokesman for Poland's Roman Catholic episcopate, Bishop Tadeusz Pieronek, also rejected the demands, saying the Church consistently upheld the need to defend life.

But even among opposition parties which have previously advocated scrapping the death penalty, partly to bring Poland into line with Western European norms as it seeks to join the European Union, some doubts were emerging.
Olga Krzyzanowska, a prominent deputy of the liberal centrist Union for Freedom (UW) said she was now considering whether the penalty should return to the statute books.

Monday's law and order march in Warsaw was the latest of more than a dozen around Poland since last year, each prompted by a senseless killing starting with that of a student thrown from a moving train by hooligans in the port city Gdansk.
Crime rates in Poland are still below those of most Western European countries and the former Soviet states but they have risen steeply since the 1989 fall of communism.
The last execution in Poland, by hanging, was carried out in 1988.
